title: Presentation Preparation
intro: You have just started work and your manager asks for a short presentation. This module shows you how to plan it, what to put on each slide, what to say, and how to handle the questions that follow.

routes.Who it's for: New graduates and anyone who has never presented at work
routes.What to do: Read all six steps, work through one scenario in full, do all 12 drills in one set

routes.Who it's for: Learners who already present in class or at work
routes.What to do: Skim the steps, read one scenario's slides and role play, do drills 1–6 (★) in one set

sessionPlan.Step: Warm-up: what does your manager actually want from you?
The six steps and the phrase bank
Scenario walk-through: read the slides and speaker script aloud
Q&A role play in pairs (swap roles once)
App drills: one set of 12 (fast track: items 1–6)
Self-score with the rubric and set one goal

steps.title: Understand the ask
steps.text: Before you open PowerPoint, confirm four things: what decision the manager needs, who else will be in the room, how long you have, and the deadline. Say: “Just to confirm, you'd like a ten-minute update on the complaints so you can decide on a fix by Friday. Is that right?”

steps.title: Write your key message in one sentence
steps.text: Use this pattern: what I found + what I recommend + what I need from you. Example: “Card complaints rose 40 percent, mainly from failed OTP payments; I recommend a four-week pilot and I need your approval today.” If you cannot write it in one sentence, you are not ready to build slides.

steps.title: Put the answer first
steps.text: This is the pyramid principle (Barbara Minto, The Pyramid Principle): give the conclusion first, then the reasons, then the detail. Managers are busy; if they only hear your first minute, they should already know your recommendation.

steps.title: Follow a simple storyline
steps.text: Situation → problem → options → recommendation → next steps. Each part becomes one slide, so a 10-minute slot has 3–5 slides.

steps.title: Build clean slides
steps.text: One idea per slide. Write the headline as a full sentence that states the point (“Complaints rose 40% in Q3”), not a label (“Complaints”). No more than three bullets. Every number shows its source and date; estimates and example figures are labelled as such.

steps.title: Rehearse and prepare for questions
steps.text: Say it aloud twice and time it. Write down the three questions you fear most and a short answer for each. Decide now what you will say if you don't know: “Let me check and get back to you by Friday.”

phraseBank.say: Thank you for your time. In the next ten minutes I'll explain why complaints rose, and I'll ask you for one decision.
My recommendation is to run a four-week pilot. There are three reasons.
Let's move on to the options. / That brings me to my second point. / To sum up this part, …
As you can see on this chart, complaints rose from 120 to 168, an increase of 40 percent.
Most of the increase came from failed OTP payments after the July upgrade.
This is an estimate based on the last three months. / These are example figures.
Option A is cheaper, but option C has the biggest impact.
If I understand correctly, you're asking whether we can do this without extra staff.
I don't have that figure with me. Let me check and get back to you by Friday.
I see your point. One thing to consider is the cost of doing nothing.
So, what I need from you today is approval for the pilot. Could we agree on that?
I'll send the slides and a one-page summary by 3 pm today.

sayThis.say: I'll update the report and send it by 3 pm.
sayThis.why: Name the action and the time. “The needful” tells the manager nothing.

sayThis.say: I'll get back to you by Friday.
sayThis.why: “Revert” already means reply in South Asian English, so “back” repeats it; outside the region “revert” means go back to an earlier state.
Discuss takes a direct object. No “about”.
“Have” for owning or holding something does not take -ing.

sayThis.say: Do you have five minutes? I'd like to update you on the complaints review.
sayThis.not: Sorry sir to disturb, can I take two minutes?
sayThis.why: Keep the respect, drop the apology. Updating your manager is your job, not a disturbance.

sayThis.say: Could you approve the pilot by Thursday?
sayThis.why: Ask a clear question with a date.
“Itself” for emphasis is local usage; it sounds unclear to overseas clients.

sayThis.say: As far as I know … / According to the March report …
sayThis.why: “As per” belongs to documents (“as per the contract”), not to what you know.

sayThis.say: Can we bring the meeting forward to 10 am?
sayThis.why: “Prepone” is understood in South Asia but not by most international managers.
In international English a doubt is a feeling of uncertainty, not a question.

sayThis.not: We are having 168 complaints this quarter.

sayThis.say: As far as I know, the penalties part has not started yet, but Legal should confirm.
sayThis.not: As per my knowledge, no fines, so no problem.
sayThis.why: Show your source and your level of certainty; never guess about the law.

sayThis.say: If we sold only 20 packets a day, we would lose about Rs 116,000 a month.
sayThis.not: If only 20 packets, loss will come.
sayThis.why: Use a full if-sentence with a number; managers trust specific answers.

bakeryFigures.item: Food and packaging cost per packet
Fixed costs per month (rider and bike Rs 120,000; kitchen helper Rs 90,000; marketing Rs 25,000)
Break-even: 235,000 ÷ 270 = 870 packets a month, over 22 working days
One-off setup (insulated boxes, ordering page, equipment)
Cumulative after setup: end of month 3 / end of month 4

scenarios.title: Customer service — why complaints rose and how to fix it
scenarios.presenter: Emma Clarke, 23, Customer Experience Executive (graduate trainee)
scenarios.manager: Mike Bennett, Head of Customer Experience
scenarios.workplace: Contact centre of a licensed commercial bank in Colombo (fictional)
scenarios.slot: 10 minutes at the Thursday team meeting, 5 slides
scenarios.brief: “Emma, card-related complaints went up last quarter. I need to know why and what we should do. You have ten minutes on Thursday. Keep it simple.” — Mike Bennett, Head of Customer Experience (role play)
scenarios.context: Real rule used: under the Central Bank of Sri Lanka's Financial Consumer Protection Regulations No. 01 of 2023, a provider must acknowledge a complaint in writing, preferably within five working days (Reg. 43.3), resolve it within 21 calendar days or tell the customer why it needs longer, up to three months (Reg. 46.1), and run root cause analysis on complaint data (Reg. 42.3). These complaint rules came into operation 12 months after 8 August 2023. All complaint counts below are example figures.
scenarios.keyMessage: Card complaints rose 40 percent last quarter, mainly from failed OTP payments after the July upgrade; I recommend a four-week pilot of two quick fixes and I need your approval today.
scenarios.outcome: Pilot approved, IT introduction made, weekly one-slide report agreed, and figures shared with Compliance.
coaching: Emma answers “Are you sure?” with the source, not with emotion.
She says “I'm not sure yet” once, with a date, and moves on.
Mike asked his team to use first names. If your workplace uses Sir or Madam, keep it; drop the apology, not the respect.

slides.headline: Card complaints rose 40% in Q3; two quick fixes can bring them down
bullets: Q2: 120 card complaints → Q3: 168 (example figures)
Main cause: failed OTP payments after the July upgrade
Today's ask: approve a four-week pilot
slides.script: Good morning, Mike, and thank you for the time. My key message is simple. Card complaints rose by 40 percent last quarter, mainly because customers could not complete online payments after the OTP change in July. I'll show you the data, three options, and at the end I'll ask you to approve a four-week pilot.

slides.headline: Failed OTP payments are the biggest driver
bullets: OTP payment failures: 70 of 168 (42%)
Card delivery delays: 48 (29%); disputed charges: 30 (18%); other: 20 (12%)
Source: complaints log, 1 July–30 September; example figures, rounded
slides.script: As you can see, failed OTP payments are the largest group, at 70 complaints, or 42 percent. Card delivery delays come second at 29 percent. Most of the increase came from the OTP group, which was very small before July.

slides.headline: We are slow at the first step of the Central Bank timeline
bullets: CBSL rules: acknowledge in writing, preferably within 5 working days; resolve within 21 calendar days
Our average time to acknowledge: 7 working days (example)
Resolved within 21 days: 82% (example)
slides.script: This is also a compliance point. The Central Bank's consumer protection rules ask us to acknowledge complaints in writing, preferably within five working days, and to resolve them within 21 calendar days. At the moment we take seven working days on average just to acknowledge.

slides.headline: Three options, from fastest to biggest impact
bullets: A: automatic SMS acknowledgement with a reference number (fast, low cost)
B: OTP help script plus a callback within 24 hours for failed payments
C: IT fix for OTP delivery delays (biggest impact, slowest, needs IT time)
slides.script: Let's move on to the options. Option A is the fastest and cheapest, and it fixes our acknowledgement time. Option B helps the customers who are affected right now. Option C fixes the root cause, but it depends on IT, so it will take longer.

slides.headline: Recommendation: pilot A and B for four weeks and raise C with IT
bullets: Week 1: set up SMS and the callback script; weeks 2–4: run and measure
Measures: OTP complaints per week, days to acknowledge, % resolved in 21 days
Ask: approve the pilot and introduce me to the IT lead
slides.script: To sum up, I recommend we pilot options A and B for four weeks and raise option C with IT now. I'll report three numbers every Friday. So, what I need from you today is approval for the pilot and an introduction to the IT lead. Could we agree on that?

questions.question: Why didn't we see this earlier?
questions.answer: OTP complaints were logged under “other” until August, so the trend was hidden. I've suggested a separate category so we can see it every week.

questions.question: Are we breaking the Central Bank rules?
questions.answer: The rule says “preferably within five working days”, so it is a target, but we are above it. Compliance should confirm our position, so I'd like to share these figures with them.

questions.question: Is the OTP problem ours or the telco's?
questions.answer: I'm not sure yet. Let me check with IT and get back to you by Friday.

questions.question: How will we know the pilot worked?
questions.answer: Three measures: OTP complaints per week, average days to acknowledge, and the share resolved within 21 days. I'll report them every Friday.

qa.title: Q&A: Customer service — why complaints rose and how to fix it
qa.setting: “Emma, card-related complaints went up last quarter. I need to know why and what we should do. You have ten minutes on Thursday. Keep it simple.” — Mike Bennett, Head of Customer Experience (role play)
qa.characters: Emma Clarke, 23, Customer Experience Executive (graduate trainee); Mike Bennett, Head of Customer Experience
qa.resolution: Pilot approved, IT introduction made, weekly one-slide report agreed, and figures shared with Compliance.

notes.text: Emma answers “Are you sure?” with the source, not with emotion.
She says “I'm not sure yet” once, with a date, and moves on.
Mike asked his team to use first names. If your workplace uses Sir or Madam, keep it; drop the apology, not the respect.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Thanks, Emma. That was really clear. But 40 percent does sound high. Are you sure about the numbers?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Yes. They come from the complaints log for July to September, and I checked them with the team leader.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Good. So, why are the OTP failures suddenly so high?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: The July upgrade changed how codes are sent. Some customers receive the code after it has expired.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Right. Is that our problem, or is it the telco's?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: I'm not sure yet. Let me check with IT and get back to you by Friday.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Okay. What will the SMS acknowledgement actually cost us?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Our current SMS package already covers it, so there's no extra cost for the pilot. Procurement confirmed that.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: And the 24-hour callback. Do we have the staff for that?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Yes, if two evening-shift agents spend one hour a day on callbacks. Their team leader has agreed.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: You've done your homework. So, what do you need from me?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Two things: approval for the four-week pilot, and an introduction to the IT lead for the OTP issue.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Approved. I'll email Daniel in IT today, and I'll copy you in.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Thank you. I'll send a one-page summary of the plan this afternoon.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: One more thing. Please share the acknowledgement figures with Compliance.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Of course. I'll send them today and copy you.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: And when will I see the first results?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Every Friday, starting next week: one slide, three numbers.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Perfect. Well done, Emma.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Thank you, Mike. I'll keep you updated.

scenarios.title: Workplace compliance — getting ready for the data protection law
scenarios.presenter: Emma Clarke, 24, Compliance and Quality Assistant
scenarios.workplace: BPO in Colombo with 220 agents serving local and overseas clients (fictional)
scenarios.slot: 10 minutes at next week's operations meeting, 5 slides
scenarios.brief: “Emma, the new data protection rules start in January and I keep hearing different things. Give me ten minutes next week: what changes for our floor, and what must we do before January?” — Mike Bennett, Operations Manager (role play)
scenarios.context: Real law used: the Personal Data Protection Act No. 9 of 2022, amended by Act No. 22 of 2025 (certified 30 October 2025). Gazette Extraordinary No. 2498/16, published 22 July 2026, appoints 1 January 2027 for Sections 2 and 3, Part I (processing of personal data) and Part III (controllers and processors, including Data Protection Officers, breach notification and impact assessments where applicable). Secondary sources report that Part II (data subject rights) and Part VII (penalties) await a further order. This scenario is a training exercise, not legal advice. Audit figures are example figures.
scenarios.keyMessage: The core of the data protection law applies to us from 1 January 2027; we have about two months, and I recommend a four-step readiness plan that needs your approval for short training slots.
scenarios.outcome: Training approved as a 20-minute huddle version, clean-desk checks start Monday, and Emma owns the Data Protection Officer question with a Friday deadline.
coaching: Emma separates what the law says, what she understands, and what Legal must confirm.
When the manager pushes back on time, she offers a smaller version instead of defending the original.
Try it yourself: present a gift and anti-bribery refresher. The Anti-Corruption Act No. 9 of 2023 made bribery in the private sector an offence (section 106).

slides.headline: From 1 January 2027 the core of the data protection law applies; we have about two months
bullets: Personal Data Protection Act No. 9 of 2022, amended in 2025
Gazette 2498/16 (22 July 2026): Parts I and III start on 1 January 2027
Today's ask: approve a four-step readiness plan
slides.script: Thank you, Mike. The short answer is: yes, the core of the data protection law starts on 1 January 2027, under a Gazette notice published in July. That gives us about two months. I'll explain what changes for the floor, where we stand, and I'll ask you to approve a four-step plan.

slides.headline: What changes: how we collect, use, keep and protect personal data
bullets: Use personal data only for a clear, lawful purpose, and only what we need
Keep it accurate, secure, and no longer than necessary
Controller and processor duties: a Data Protection Officer, breach reporting and impact assessments, where applicable
slides.script: In plain English, the law asks us to use personal data only for a clear purpose, collect only what we need, keep it accurate and secure, and not keep it longer than necessary. Part III also covers Data Protection Officers, breach reporting and impact assessments. Legal will need to confirm exactly which duties apply to each client contract.

slides.headline: Where we stand today: habits are the main gap
bullets: Last data protection training: 18 months ago (example)
Spot check: customer details on paper notes at 9 of 40 desks (example)
No single list of the personal data each process holds
slides.script: Here is where we stand. Our last training was 18 months ago. In last week's spot check, nine of the 40 desks I visited had customer details on paper notes. And we have no single list of what personal data each process holds. The main gap is habits, not knowledge.

slides.headline: Four steps before January
bullets: 1. Data map per client process, with Legal and team leaders (3 weeks)
2. Confirm our Data Protection Officer and the breach reporting route
3. Short refresher and quiz for all 220 agents; 4. weekly clean-desk checks
slides.script: I propose four steps. First, a data map for each client process. Second, confirm who our Data Protection Officer is and how agents report a suspected breach. Third, a short refresher with a quiz for every agent, so we have a record. Fourth, weekly clean-desk checks by team leaders.

slides.headline: What I need from you
bullets: Approve 30-minute training slots across all shifts (about 110 agent-hours)
Nominate one team leader per shift as data champion
Raise the Data Protection Officer question with the Head of Legal
slides.script: So, what I need from you today is three things: approval for the training slots, one team leader per shift as a data champion, and your help to raise the Data Protection Officer question with the Head of Legal. Could we agree on those?

questions.question: Will we be fined if we're not ready on 1 January?
questions.answer: From what I've read, the penalties part has not been brought into operation yet; it needs a further order. But I'm not a lawyer, so I'd like Legal to confirm. Either way, our clients will expect us to comply from January.

questions.question: Our clients are overseas. Does this law even apply?
questions.answer: My understanding is that it covers personal data processed wholly or partly in Sri Lanka, so it is likely to apply to our work. Legal should confirm it for each contract; that's part of step one.

questions.question: Can't we just send an email instead of training?
questions.answer: An email is quick, but the spot check shows the problem is habits. A short session with a quiz changes behaviour and gives us a record that everyone completed it.

questions.question: How much floor time will this cost?
questions.answer: 220 agents times 30 minutes is about 110 agent-hours. Spread over two weeks and all shifts, it is about one agent per team per day.

qa.title: Q&A: Workplace compliance — getting ready for the data protection law
qa.setting: “Emma, the new data protection rules start in January and I keep hearing different things. Give me ten minutes next week: what changes for our floor, and what must we do before January?” — Mike Bennett, Operations Manager (role play)
qa.characters: Emma Clarke, 24, Compliance and Quality Assistant; Mike Bennett, Operations Manager
qa.resolution: Training approved as a 20-minute huddle version, clean-desk checks start Monday, and Emma owns the Data Protection Officer question with a Friday deadline.

notes.text: Emma separates what the law says, what she understands, and what Legal must confirm.
When the manager pushes back on time, she offers a smaller version instead of defending the original.
Try it yourself: present a gift and anti-bribery refresher. The Anti-Corruption Act No. 9 of 2023 made bribery in the private sector an offence (section 106).

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Thanks, Emma. So, the law really starts in January?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Yes. The core parts start on 1 January 2027, under a Gazette notice published in July.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Which parts, exactly? I don't want us to over-react.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: The rules on processing personal data, and the duties of controllers and processors. The penalties part has not started yet.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Then why the rush?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Because the duties apply from January, and our clients will audit us against them.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Fair point. But 30 minutes for 220 agents is a lot of floor time.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: I understand. It's about 110 agent-hours. We could spread it over two weeks, across all shifts.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Could you do it in 20 minutes, during team huddles?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Yes, if I cut the theory and keep the quiz. I'll send you the new version by Wednesday.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Good. And who is our Data Protection Officer?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: That's the one thing I couldn't confirm. Let me check with Legal and get back to you by Friday.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Please do. And what about the paper notes on the desks?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Team leaders can do a two-minute clean-desk check at each shift change.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Agreed. Let's start that on Monday.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: I will. Shall I send a one-page plan to the team leaders?

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Send it to me first, and I'll forward it.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Of course. You'll have it by 4 pm today.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Thank you. This was clear, and it was practical.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Thank you, Mike. I'll update you after I meet Legal.

scenarios.title: Business plan — a corporate lunch delivery line
scenarios.workplace: Family-owned bakery and café chain with three outlets in Kandy (fictional)
scenarios.slot: 10–15 minutes at the monthly management meeting, 5 slides
scenarios.brief: “Emma, offices near our Peradeniya Road outlet keep asking for lunch packets. Give me a simple business plan for a corporate lunch delivery line. I need to know whether it's worth trying.” — Mike Bennett, General Manager (role play)
scenarios.context: Why it matters: small and medium-sized enterprises are widely reported to produce more than half of Sri Lanka's GDP and about 45 percent of employment (ADB sector assessment, citing the Ministry of Finance), so many graduates will present plans to owner-managers like Mike. Every price, cost and volume below is an example figure for practice, not market data.
scenarios.keyMessage: A corporate lunch line could add about Rs 240,000 a month in profit at 80 packets a day; break-even is about 40 a day, so I recommend a three-month pilot with a clear stop rule.
scenarios.outcome: A smaller pilot is approved: two months, Rs 300,000 maximum, five offices, weekly numbers, and the same stop rule.
coaching: Emma expected the cost objection and had a cheaper option ready.
She explains break-even in one sentence, without jargon.
A smaller yes is a good result. Accept it, confirm the terms, and say what happens next.

slides.headline: A lunch delivery line could add about Rs 240,000 a month; I recommend a three-month pilot
bullets: Demand already exists: five nearby offices have asked
Break-even at about 40 packets a day; target 80 (example figures)
Today's ask: Rs 450,000 setup budget and a three-month pilot
slides.script: Thank you, Mike. My recommendation is a three-month pilot of a corporate lunch delivery line. At 80 packets a day it could add about 240,000 rupees a month in profit. These are example figures, and I'll show you how I calculated them. At the end, I'll ask you for a setup budget of 450,000 rupees.

slides.headline: The demand: nearby offices are already asking
bullets: Five offices near Peradeniya Road asked in the last two months (example)
About 400 staff in those offices; if one in five orders, that's 80 a day
Competition: delivery apps and office canteens
slides.script: Here is the demand. Five offices near our Peradeniya Road outlet have asked for lunch packets in the last two months. Together they have about 400 staff. If one in five orders, that is 80 packets a day. That is an assumption, and the pilot is how we test it.

slides.headline: The numbers: break-even is about 40 packets a day
bullets: Price Rs 650; food and packaging Rs 380; margin Rs 270 per packet
Fixed costs Rs 235,000 a month: rider and bike, kitchen helper, marketing
Setup Rs 450,000; payback in month 4 if sales build to 80 a day
slides.script: Each packet sells for 650 rupees and costs 380 to make, so we keep 270. Our fixed costs are 235,000 rupees a month, so we need about 40 packets a day to break even. If sales build from 30 to 80 a day over three months, we pay back the setup cost in the fourth month.

slides.headline: Three risks, and how we'll manage them
bullets: Demand is lower than expected: stop if under 40 a day by the end of month two
Late delivery in rain: covered bike box and a 12:30 delivery promise
Food safety: confirm our licence and hygiene checks cover delivery
slides.script: There are three main risks. The biggest is demand, so I propose a clear stop rule: if we average under 40 packets a day by the end of month two, we close the pilot. For delivery, we promise 12:30, not a ten-minute slot. And we'll confirm our licence and hygiene checks cover delivery before we start.

slides.headline: The ask: Rs 450,000 and a three-month pilot with five offices
bullets: Start with the five offices that asked
Weekly report: packets sold, revenue, complaints
Go or stop decision at the end of month two
slides.script: To sum up: the demand is there, break-even is about 40 a day, and we have a stop rule if it doesn't work. So, I'd like your approval for 450,000 rupees and a three-month pilot with the five offices. Could we agree on that today?

questions.question: What if we sell only 20 packets a day?
questions.answer: Then we would lose about Rs 116,000 a month, because 440 packets × Rs 270 is Rs 118,800 against Rs 235,000 of fixed costs. That's why the plan has a stop rule at the end of month two.

questions.question: Where did 80 a day come from?
questions.answer: From the five offices: about 400 staff, and I assumed one in five orders. It's an assumption, so the pilot is designed to test it.

questions.question: Can the kitchen cope?
questions.answer: Yes, with one extra helper from 9 am to 1 pm. The head chef has reviewed the plan.

questions.question: Why Rs 650? Canteens are cheaper.
questions.answer: We're selling convenience and our brand, not the cheapest meal. I'd like to test the price in the first month and adjust if orders are low.

qa.title: Q&A: Business plan — a corporate lunch delivery line
qa.setting: “Emma, offices near our Peradeniya Road outlet keep asking for lunch packets. Give me a simple business plan for a corporate lunch delivery line. I need to know whether it's worth trying.” — Mike Bennett, General Manager (role play)
qa.characters: Emma Clarke, 22, Business Development Trainee; Mike Bennett, General Manager
qa.resolution: A smaller pilot is approved: two months, Rs 300,000 maximum, five offices, weekly numbers, and the same stop rule.

notes.text: Emma expected the cost objection and had a cheaper option ready.
She explains break-even in one sentence, without jargon.
A smaller yes is a good result. Accept it, confirm the terms, and say what happens next.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Interesting, Emma. But Rs 450,000 is a lot for a test.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: I understand. Most of it is for insulated boxes and the ordering page.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Could we start a bit smaller?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Yes. If we take orders on WhatsApp instead of building a page, the setup drops to about Rs 300,000.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: That's better. And if the offices don't order?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Then we stop. If we average under 40 packets a day by the end of month two, we close the pilot.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Why 40?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: That's our break-even point. Below 40 a day, the line loses money.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: And who delivers when it rains?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: The rider will have a covered bike box, and we'll promise delivery by 12:30, not a ten-minute slot.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Have you spoken to the chef?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Yes. He agreed, if we add one helper from 9 to 1.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: All right. Two months, and Rs 300,000 maximum.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Thank you. Shall I start with the five offices that asked?

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Yes. And send me the numbers every week.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: I will. Every Monday: packets sold, revenue and complaints.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: When can you start?

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: In two weeks, once the boxes arrive.

lines.name: Mike
lines.text: Fine. That was well presented.

lines.name: Emma
lines.text: Thank you, Mike. I'll send the revised plan tomorrow.

items.question: My ____ is that we run a four-week pilot.
items.explanation: After “my” you need a noun: recommendation.

items.question: Which is the best opening?
options: Today I am going to discuss about complaints.
Sorry sir to disturb, I will tell some things about complaints.
Thank you for your time. In the next ten minutes, I'll explain why complaints rose and what I recommend.
items.explanation: Thank the manager, give the time, and say what they will get. No apology, and no “discuss about”.

items.question: Put your main message ____: managers want the answer before the detail.
items.explanation: Answer first: this is the pyramid principle.

items.question: Which is the best slide headline?
options: Complaints rose 40% in Q3, mainly from OTP failures
items.explanation: A headline should state the point as a full sentence, not a label.

items.question: For a 10-minute slot, plan about ____ slides.
items.explanation: About two minutes a slide: 3–5 slides fit ten minutes.

items.question: Which sentence best confirms the manager's ask?
options: OK sir, I will do the needful.
What you want me to do?
Just to confirm, you'd like a ten-minute update so you can decide on the pilot by Friday?
items.explanation: Repeat back the purpose, the time and the decision. “The needful” confirms nothing.

items.question: That brings me ____ my second point.
items.explanation: The fixed phrase is “brings me to”.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Let's move on to the options.
items.explanation: Move on to + noun; after “let's” use the base verb.

items.question: Each slide should carry ____ main idea.
items.explanation: One idea per slide keeps the manager focused.

items.question: Which is the best way to close?
options: So, what I need from you today is approval for the pilot.
items.explanation: End with a clear ask. Say “Any questions?”, not “Any doubts?”.

items.question: To ____ up, the pilot is low cost and quick to test.
items.explanation: The phrase is “to sum up”.

items.question: Which follow-up promise is best?
options: I will revert back with slides.
I'll send the slides and a one-page summary by 3 pm.
items.explanation: Say what you will send and when.

items.question: Complaints rose ____ 120 to 168.
items.explanation: Rise from X to Y.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We are had 168 complaints this quarter.
We are having 168 complaints this quarter.
items.explanation: Have (own, hold) does not take -ing; the quarter is finished, so use the past.

items.question: That is an increase ____ 40 percent.
items.explanation: The noun “increase” takes “of” before the amount.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
items.explanation: The verb “increase” takes “by” before the amount.

items.question: Most of the increase came ____ failed OTP payments.
items.explanation: Something comes from a source or cause.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: As you can see on this chart, OTP failures is the largest group.
As you are seeing this chart, OTP failures are largest group.
As you can see on this chart, OTP failures are the largest group.
items.explanation: Failures is plural, so use “are”; keep “the” before a superlative.

items.question: These figures ____ from the complaints log for July to September.
items.explanation: Figures is plural: these figures come.

items.question: Which sentence reports the CBSL rule accurately?
options: Central Bank is telling to acknowledge in five days.
The Central Bank asks banks to acknowledge complaints in writing, preferably within five working days.
The Central Bank says complaints must be fully solved in five days.
items.explanation: The regulation says acknowledge, preferably within five working days; resolution is 21 calendar days.

items.question: Option A is cheaper ____ option C.
items.explanation: Comparatives take “than”. “Then” is about time.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Option B is more faster than option C.
Option B is faster than option C.
Option B is fastest than option C.
items.explanation: Short adjectives add -er; never use “more” and -er together.

items.question: If I understand ____, you're asking about the cost.
items.explanation: An adverb describes the verb “understand”.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We discussed the OTP problem with IT.
We discussed on the OTP problem with IT.
We discussed about the OTP problem with IT.
items.explanation: Discuss takes a direct object: no “about” or “on”.

items.question: The core provisions come into operation ____ 1 January 2027.
items.explanation: Use “on” with a date.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The law will comes into force in 1 January 2027.
The law has came into force.
The law comes into force on 1 January 2027.
items.explanation: Has come (not came); will come (not comes); on a date.

items.question: We should keep only the personal data we ____.
items.explanation: We need: no -s after “we”.

items.question: Which is the best way to talk about something you're unsure of?
options: My understanding is that the penalties part has not started yet, but Legal should confirm.
Penalties are 100% not there, no problem.
I think no fines, so we can relax.
items.explanation: Say what you understand and who will confirm it. Never guess about the law.

items.question: Agents ____ report a suspected data breach to their team leader immediately.
items.explanation: Modal verbs (should, must) take the base verb with no “to”.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Every agents have to complete the training by 15 December.
Every agent have to complete the training by 15 December.
Every agent has to complete the training by 15 December.
items.explanation: Every + singular noun + singular verb (has).

items.question: I couldn't confirm who our DPO is. Let me check with Legal and get ____ to you by Friday.
items.explanation: Get back to you = reply to you. Avoid “revert back”.

items.question: Which request is clearest?
options: Kindly do the needful regarding the training slots.
Could you approve two 20-minute training slots per shift?
items.explanation: Ask a direct question with the exact thing you need.

items.question: The spot check found customer details ____ paper notes at 9 of 40 desks.
items.explanation: Writing is on paper or on a note.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I am not having the latest client list.
I don't have the latest client list with me.
I am not have the latest client list.
items.explanation: Have (own, hold) is not used in the continuous; use don't have.

items.question: This is not legal advice; it is a summary ____ the main changes.
items.explanation: A summary of something.

items.question: Which sentence is most professional?
options: As far as I know, some organisations need a DPO, and Legal will confirm whether we do.
According to me knowledge, DPO is must.
As per my knowledge, DPO is a must.
items.explanation: “As far as I know” shows your level of certainty; “as per” is for documents.

drillSets.title: Numbers, risks and the ask (business plan)

items.question: Our break-even point is about 40 packets ____ day.
items.explanation: 40 a day (or 40 per day).

items.question: Which sentence labels the figures correctly?
options: These are example figures, not actual sales.
items.explanation: Always label example or estimated figures as such.

items.question: If we sold 80 packets a day, we ____ make about Rs 240,000 a month.
items.explanation: If + past simple, would + base verb: a possible result.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I recommend that we run a three-month pilot.
I recommend to run a three-month pilot.
I am recommending you to run pilot.
items.explanation: Recommend that we + base verb (or recommend running).

items.question: The main ____ is that demand may be lower than we expect.
items.explanation: After “the main” you need a noun.

items.question: Choose the clearest request.
options: Can we bring the launch forward to next week?
Can we pre-pone forward the launch?
Let's prepone the launch to next week.
items.explanation: Bring forward is understood everywhere; prepone is local usage.

items.question: The pilot will cost ____ than a full launch.
items.explanation: Less for amounts (money, cost); fewer for things you count.

items.question: Which is the best answer to “What if sales are low?”
options: If we sold only 20 packets a day, we would lose about Rs 116,000 a month, so we would stop the pilot.
items.explanation: Answer what-if questions with a number and a plan.

items.question: We will stop the pilot ____ sales are below 40 packets a day by the end of month two.
items.explanation: If introduces the condition for stopping.

items.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The numbers are based on the assumption that one in five staff will order.
The numbers are based in assumption one of five staffs will order.
items.explanation: Based on; staff has no -s; one in five.

items.question: Could we ____ on a budget of Rs 300,000?
items.explanation: After could use the base verb.

items.question: Which is the best close?
options: So, please give approval if possible if not ok.
So, I'd like your approval for a two-month pilot with a budget of Rs 300,000.
items.explanation: Close with a clear ask: what, how much, how long.

levels.1: Main point unclear, or only at the end
levels.3: Point stated, but after long background
levels.5: Key message in one sentence in the first minute

levels.3: Logical order, weak links between slides
levels.5: Situation, problem, options, recommendation, next steps, with signposts

levels.1: Numbers with no source or date
levels.5: Every number sourced and dated; estimates labelled
Plain professional English; no “do the needful” or “revert back”
Checks the question, answers briefly, admits gaps with a date
On time; speaks to the manager, not the screen
